episodes.159118: An area of high pressure remained centered over the Four Corners while a slow-moving low pressure system tracked westward across southern New Mexico on July 22, 2021. Above normal atmospheric moisture values remained across much of central and western New Mexico which helped to set the stage for an active monsoon day across the area. The risk for flash flooding was highest across western New Mexico where steering flow was slow and the potential for training storms was high. Heavy thunderstorms in southern Catron County produced heavy rainfall in the area. Flash flooding was reported in Old Horse Springs where multiple homes were flooded and county roads were washed out.
episodes.159225: With above normal atmospheric moisture values in place across northern and central New Mexico, it was another active monsoon day on July 21, 2021. The greatest storm coverage was across north central and west central New Mexico where numerous thunderstorms developed throughout the afternoon and evening hours. With the above normal moisture values and slow steering flow, heavy rain was common with these thunderstorms. A thunderstorm near Chaco Canyon produced significant flash flooding which damaged the park and forced its closure for several days.
episodes.159337: Several individual thunderstorms produced wind gusts of 34 knots or more as they moved across north Merritt Island, from the Indian River to the nearshore Atlantic.
episodes.159623: Even with high pressure centered over the region, deep monsoonal moisture continued to advect into western Colorado. In addition to the well above normal precipitable water values across the area, the passage of a subtle shortwave trough resulted in the development of widespread showers and thunderstorms. Some storms produced heavy rain which led to debris flows including across portions of the Grizzly Creek Fire burn scar.
episodes.159669: Strong west-southwest winds of 40-50kts occurred around 500mb. Lower/mid-tropospheric lapse rates were steep in response to insolation and weak mid-level cooling. In addition, there was sufficient low-level moisture to support weak to modest|CAPE on the order of 500-1000 J/kg. This resulted in the development of thunderstorms which produced mainly severe wind gusts.
episodes.159729: Moist SW steering flow produced another day of sea breeze storms with a merger focused toward the I-95 corridor in the afternoon where a few pulse severe storms occurred.
episodes.159744: A subtle pulse of monsoon moisture worked its way northward across western Colorado. This, paired with the already present abundance of moisture, resulted in scattered showers and thunderstorms across the region. The stronger storms produced heavy rain, some of which led to localized debris flows in Pitkin and San Juan counties.
episodes.159843: Clusters of strong thunderstorms developed along a cold front in the afternoon hours across southeast South Carolina. These thunderstorms became strong enough to produce strong wind gusts.
episodes.159991: The environment had all the ingredients for strong to severe storms including above normal moisture and forecast shear in excess of 40 miles per hour, conducive to wind and hail threats.
episodes.160555: Strong thunderstorms over far southeast Montana developed into a line of severe thunderstorms as they tracked across northwestern South Dakota. Wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were common within the line, with localized gusts as high as 90 mph.
episodes.160877: Heavy rain produced a debris flow that impacted CO-125 near Mile Marker 7 in the East Troublesome burn area. A USFS vehicle was entrapped in a mud/debris flow on Cabin Creek Road. It partially buried his vehicle. The employee was safe and uninjured.  Localized flash flooding also occurred along Kinney Creek in the Williams Fork burn area.
episodes.160985: An unstable southwesterly flow developed ahead of an approaching Pacific trough and brought strong to severe thunderstorms over a three day period.  Surface based CAPE routinely exceeded 1000 j/kg as steep mid-level lapse rates above 8C/km were common. Dry sub-cloud layers helped produce strong thunderstorm wind gusts and effective shear well above 30 kts was enough for quarter size hail and larger. The peak in severe weather occurred on Wednesday July 21st as the main energy associated with the trough moved through the region.
episodes.161245: An active monsoon surge brought several back-to-back days of thunderstorms producing heavy rain, damaging wind gusts, and hail across the state.
episodes.161306: Thunderstorms developed ahead of a surface low and approaching short-wave trough. Some of these thunderstorms produced severe wind gusts. The strongest gust occurred near Center in Oliver County, with estimated winds of 70 mph.
episodes.161391: A big push of monsoon moisture led to ten days of scattered thunderstorms over the Mojave Desert. Many storms produced flash flooding and/or high winds. Events in this episode are continued in the July 22-26 Thunderstorms episode.
episodes.161392: A big push of monsoon moisture led to five days of scattered thunderstorms over the Mojave Desert and the Sierra. Many storms produced flash flooding and/or high winds.
episodes.161407: A cold front exiting southeast Massachusetts in the evening on July 21st caused an isolated thunderstorm to become marginally severe in Randolph, MA.
episodes.161478: Monsoonal thunderstorm activity occurred across Southern California from July 22 to July 29, with a major easterly wave producing widespread convection on July 25 and 26. Numerous reports of heavy rain leading to flash flooding and debris flows were received as well as reports of lightning, hail and dust storm.
episodes.161489: The weather pattern across the region directed strong upper-level winds and a marginally unstable atmosphere into an area of plentiful moisture that sustained multiple severe thunderstorms through the afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.161510: This is a continuation of the July 17-21 Thunderstorms episode, which lasted ten days total.
episodes.161596: An abundance of moisture and instability, focus for thunderstorm development over and near the mountains, and slow moving storms all supported heavy rainfall with flash flooding. Multiple reports were noted along the eastern mountains.
episodes.161611: A number of rounds of thunderstorms were triggered by a westward moving upper level weather system across southeast Arizona from the afternoon of July 22 into the early morning of July 23. Thunderstorms produced wind damage and flash flooding in Douglas, Green Valley and the Tucson Metro area. Flooding also occurred along the San Pedro River as well as the Pantano Wash and Rillito River, and eventually downstream along the Santa Cruz River. In Graham County, 1 fatality occurred in a flash flood of the Cottonwood Wash near Pima on July 22.
episodes.161624: With enhanced easterlies on the south end of the monsoon high and embedded weak perturbation waves rolling west across southern Arizona, scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed in a moist unstable environment throughout the afternoon and evening on the 21st. Most storms in the afternoon developed across southwest Arizona, between Phoenix and the Colorado River, with sporadic storm motions driven by outflows and cell mergers. In the evening, new showers and thunderstorms developed and spread through south-central Arizona, including in the Phoenix metro area. With high moisture content and strong forcing, thunderstorms produced very heavy rain with rainfall rates around 1.5-2.0 inches per hour with briefly higher rates for short periods. Thunderstorms also produced damaging winds, which generated dense blowing dust in open desert areas. One storm produced a severe microburst in the small town of Tacna in Yuma county that caused significant damage. The American Red Cross Disaster Relief and Yuma County Sheriffs Office was called in to support those impacted by the storm.
episodes.161629: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed in an unstable atmosphere in the afternoon of the 22nd. Storms initially developed over the high terrain of northern and eastern Arizona as well as near the Table Top mesa area south of Phoenix. High DCAPE promoted strong thunderstorm downbursts. The downbursts generated outflows that progressed into the greater Phoenix metro area and led to the development of additional scattered thunderstorm. The thunderstorms in the metro area produced damaging winds that led to numerous downed trees, downed power poles, and other property damage. The storms were also nearly stationary, under weak steering flow, and produced very heavy rainfall with rain rates around 1.5-2.0 inches per hour and briefly higher in the strongest storms. This led to considerable flash flooding around Phoenix with several road closure and significant flow in major washes. Even after the strongest storms in Phoenix subsided in the late evening of the 22nd, areas of moderate to heavy rain continued from northeast to southwest through the night and through mid-afternoon on the 23rd. The continued rain through the 23rd was aided by a strengthening diffluent flow regime between the monsoon high to the north and a retrograding upper low moving west through New Mexico. Additional significant flash flooding was observed on the 23rd, mostly in the foothills north of the Phoenix metro, with many road closures, flowing washes and creeks, and some water rescues.
episodes.161705: An isolated waterspout was observed near Sunset Key in association with a convective cloud line along the extreme lower Florida Keys.
episodes.161770: A strong thunderstorm associated with cold front that moved across the state through the day continued to move off the coast of New Hampshire and produced a 34 knot wind gust on the Isle of Shoals.
episodes.162103: High pressure centered over The Four Corners area brought a moist southerly flow over northern Arizona. This allowed thunderstorms with heavy rain to form over parts of northern Arizona resulting in several flash floods.
episodes.162106: Deep monsoon moisture remained over northern Arizona with several flash floods form the heavy rain.

events.narrative: Thunderstorm winds blew over two travel trailers in Golden Valley.
Havasu Creek at Supai rose 18 inches in about an hour. It took six hours for the creek to return to normal.
Water flowed over Stockton Hill Road.
A long-lived severe storm continued to produce 1 hail east of Seeley Lake. Additionally, it was reported the storm was producing heavy rain and winds up to 40 mph.

Hassayampa River Preserve closed several trails due to water/debris with a sudden rise in the Hassayampa River. Palm Lake in the reserve reportedly rose by 3 feet due to flood waters and video from the day after the heavy rain showed evidence of 1-3 feet of flow in the typically dry river bed. A USGS streamflow gage a few miles downstream measured a rapid 1 foot rise in 30 minutes. No damages or injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds damaged fences, roofs, trees, power lines, and an awning.
Water and debris flowed over Aztec Road and Bacobi Road near Shinarump Drive.
Heavy rainfall of 1.92 inches.
Water flowed over Gordon Drive.
In Randolph, a large limb was down at the intersection of Dorr Street and Vinton Street. |Power lines were down at Dorr and Russ Street.  Time approximate based on radar.

This particular thunderstorm developed off the outflow boundary from a previous severe storm affecting Missoula and Powell Counties. The FBAN on the Anderson Hill Fire reported large hail and heavy rain had fallen on the fire. In fact, he said sufficient hail had fallen to cover the ground white. The storm continued to Monture Ranger Station where a ranger reported 2 hail and damage to vehicle windscreens (unknown number of vehicles).
A significant debris flow of mud, rocks and branches occurred on Cinnamon Pass in the San Juan Mountains. The exact time of the slide is unknown.
A Capitol Reef National Park official shared a video of flash flooding in Sulphur Creek.
The Wendover Port of Entry automated weather station recorded a peak wind gust of 64 mph.

Heavy rain and extreme flash flooding impacted Chaco Canyon National Historical Park. Damage to roadways, including the north and south entrances to the park, was reported along with damages to the Gallo campground. One individual attempted to drive through the flooded road which prompted a successful water rescue. Due to the flooding and damages, the park was forced to close for several days. Damages are estimated.
Flash flooding occurred at County lane 6 and Jauvez road in Ft. Garland. Significant torrents of water carved out the road in places.
Forest service tower staff reported quarter sized hail (1 inch in diameter).
Co-Op observer reported 1 inch hail.
KHVR measured a 50 kt (58 mph) thunderstorm wind gust.
Thunderstorm winds blew down six power poles. Multiple vehicles were stuck.

events.narrative: A 34 knot wind gust occurred at the Isle of Shoals.
Heavy rainfall of 1.75 inches.
The Paria - Kanab gauge on the Paria River indicated a rise to 519 CFS, or about 1.5 feet.
Table of rainfall amounts over 7 days across the El Dorado and Apple Burn Scars. Three locations received over 1 inch in 7 days.
Public reported ping pong size hail.  Time estimated from radar.
Public reported 2 inches of rain fell during a two hour period.  The rain came in two waves with most of it falling during the first 30 minutes.  Time estimated from radar.
Multiple well established cottonwood trees on a property, ranging from 30 to 40 feet tall and 1 to 3 feet in diameter were uprooted or blown over.  Estimated wind was 70mph.
An observer in Bryce Canyon National Park reported hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.
Tree limbs 6 inches in diameter were broken.
Mesonet Station MTBVR measured a wind gust of 69mph.
A wind gust of 73mph was reported at the Mesonet Station MTBVR.  This was higher than a previous wind gust reported earlier.
KBZN measured a 59 kt (68 mph) thunderstorm wind gust.
A medium sized out building was flipped over by thunderstorm wind gusts, some tree damage was reported as well.
A weather spotter reported water running down streets in Tropic.
A lightning bolt blew a four foot wide hole through the roof of a St. George home starting a fire. No one was hurt.

Beaver County dispatch and emergency management personnel reported street flooding in Milford with water 3 feet deep. In addition, debris from flooding was reported on State Route 21 near Milford. The Milford automated weather station recorded 1.10 inches of rain in one hour.

Damage occurred from south of Green Valley northward up Boulder Highway, and included numerous trees down, six to eight power poles down, major power lines down, and at least one parking awning damaged.

The Catron County emergency manager reported that heavy rain in Old Horse Springs resulted in flash flooding across the area. A local resident measured 3.5 inches of rain in just 45 minutes. This resulted in multiple barns and homes in the area flooded as well as the local fire department. The emergency manager also reported that several county roads had been washed away. Damages are estimated.
A picture of a fallen tree was shared on social media by a local broadcast station. The tree fell on a powerline on Thomas Hamilton Road.

Warm Springs was closed between Arroyo Grande and Valle Verde, water covered the intersection of Sunset and Stephanie, and the onramp from Sunset onto Interstate 515 southbound was flooded a foot deep with two cars stalled.
The spotter estimated wind gusts at 60 mph.
Wind gusts were estimated near 70 mph.
Heavy rain produced localized flash flooding along Kinney Creek.  There was some damage to the road.  The floodwaters also impacted nearby properties.

Heavy rain produced a debris flow that impacted CO-125 near Mile Marker 7.  County Road 21 was also flooded near its confluence.  The debris flow forced the closure of the highway until it could be cleared.  A mud/debris flow in the Cabin Creek drainage partially buried a parked USFS vehicle, and trapped the employee behind a washed-out road. The Forest Service employee was assessing one of the closed forest service roads when the storm hit, he was found safe and uninjured.
Nottingham Road west of Buck Creek Road in Avon was closed for several hours after multiple mudslides occurred as a result of heavy rains.
Widespread standing water and urban flooding was reported in Richfield. Radar estimates indicated 1-1.25 inches of rain over a brief period.
Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument officials reported flash flooding along the Escalante River and Calf Creek.
The Paria - Kanab gauge on the Paria River indicated a 3 foot rise, with peak flows of 1800 CFS.
Hail up to 3/4 inch in diameter reported by a trained spotter visiting the area.

Heavy rain of 0.5 inch. Spotter report of a heavy downpour near Jacumba for 10-15 minutes with 2-3 inches of water on the patio, and about 2 feet of water on sections of the dirt road leading to his home.
Capitol Reef National Park officials reported flash flooding in Sheets Gulch.
Flash flooding was reported in main side canyons that flow into Marble Canyon and the Colorado River just west of Navajo Bridge. The two named side canyons were Soap Creek and Jackass.

events.narrative: A Weatherflow mesonet site at Parrish Park in Titusville (XFAR) adjacent to the Indian River measured a wind gust of 35 knots from west as a thunderstorm moved from the mainland to the river.
Wind gusts were estimated at 60 mph.
The spotter estimated wind gusts at 60 mph.

Heavy rain formed over the Grizzly Creek burn scar near Glenwood Springs, CO which caused a major mudslide across the Colorado River near MM 124 of Interstate 70. According to CDOT, the material in the river resulted in some damming of the river. Additionally, a smaller mudslide occurred at MM 129 at the same time and flowed across I-70 with an unknown depth. I-70 was closed for an extended period due to cleanup operations.

Multiple RVs were damaged or displaced after strong to severe winds impacted the Sonoran Desert RV Park. 10 RVs were moved 5 to 6 feet and one was knocked over on its side. Additionally, one RV had windows broken and another had a cracked glass door. Winds estimated based on damage and timing based on radar. No injuries were reported.
A pine tree was blown down near the intersection of State Road 121 and southern State Nursery Road. The tree was about 6 inches in diameter. The time of damage was based on radar.

events.narrative: A mesonet site (FW0175) located in northern Merritt Island adjacent to the Indian River measured a wind gust of 34 knots from northwest as a thunderstorm moved onshore from the Indian River.
Trees were uprooted and snapped near State Road 121 and Jeff Starling Road.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near the intersection of Speedway and Craycroft, which led to a traffic accident.

Heavy rain from a thunderstorm caused flooding on State Route 260 on the south side of Show Low. A car got stuck in the high water.  Flooding was also reported east of Show Low near Highway 60 and Little Mormon Lake Road meet and on to the Second Knoll Shooting Range (Forest Road 206).
Turkey Creek overflowed it's bank and flooded a road south of Lowder Street.

events.narrative: A waterspout was observed west of Key West, near Sunset Key.  No spray ring was observed.
Wind gusts were estimated at 60 mph.

One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour over east central Tucson caused flash flooding along and near Alamo Wash.  A child was rescued from flood waters near 22nd and Kolb.  Farther north, Alamo Wash overtopped Speedway Blvd and Sahuara Ave.
